## Overview

An **organic acid** is a carbon-containing compound that can donate a proton, and an **organic base** is a carbon-containing compound that can accept a proton — but the two classes are far more diverse than the simple definitions suggest. The most important organic acids are the **carboxylic acids** (general formula \( \text{RCOOH} \), pKa ≈ 4–5), **phenols** (pKa ≈ 10), and **alcohols** (pKa ≈ 16–18). The most important organic bases are the **amines** (general formula \( \text{R}_3\text{N} \), whose conjugate acids have pKa ≈ 10–11). What makes organic acids and bases interesting is that their strength is *tunable*: structural features such as electronegativity, resonance, hybridization, and inductive effects change pKa values by many orders of magnitude. Understanding why acetic acid is about \( 10^{11} \) times more acidic than ethanol — both contain an O–H bond — is the payoff of this topic. This chapter section also introduces **acidic and basic sites within the same molecule**, such as amino acids, which carry both a carboxylic acid and an amine group.

## Why This Matters

- **Drug chemistry:** most drugs are weak acids or weak bases, and their ionization state (set by pKa and pH) determines whether they dissolve in water, cross membranes, or bind to receptors. Aspirin (acid, pKa 3.5), ibuprofen (acid, pKa 4.9), and many antidepressants (amines) are classic examples.
- **Enzyme and metabolic biochemistry:** the amino acid side chains — carboxylates, ammonium groups, imidazole of histidine, phenol of tyrosine — do the acid–base work inside enzyme active sites.
- **Synthesis:** protonating an alcohol converts it into a good leaving group (\( \text{ROH}_2^+ \)); deprotonating an alkyne or amine generates a powerful nucleophile. Acid–base chemistry is the first step of countless mechanisms.
- **Everyday science:** why acetic acid in vinegar is a weak acid while HCl is strong, why amine salts (like ammonium chloride) are water-soluble solids, and why soap works better in basic conditions.

## Core Concepts

### The three major families of organic acids

| Family | Example structure | Typical pKa | Why the conjugate base is stabilized |
|---|---|---|---|
| Carboxylic acid | \( \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \) (acetic acid) | 4.76 | **Resonance:** the carboxylate ion \( \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- \) delocalizes the negative charge over two equivalent oxygens |
| Phenol | \( \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \) | ~10 | **Resonance into the ring:** the phenoxide ion delocalizes charge onto ortho/para ring carbons |
| Alcohol | \( \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \) (ethanol) | ~16 | No resonance; the alkoxide ion \( \text{RO}^- \) carries the full negative charge on one oxygen |

The pattern to internalize: **the more the conjugate base spreads out its negative charge, the more stable it is, and the more acidic the parent acid.** Acetic acid's conjugate base shares charge between two oxygens (resonance), so acetic acid is far more acidic than ethanol, whose conjugate base localizes charge on a single oxygen.

### What makes a base strong: the conjugate acid test

Basicity is measured by the pKa of the **conjugate acid**. The higher the pKa of \( \text{BH}^+ \), the stronger the base B. Amines have conjugate acids with pKa ≈ 10–11 (\( \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+ \), pKa 10.6), so alkylamines are strong organic bases. Structural changes that stabilize the conjugate acid (or destabilize the lone pair) raise basicity; changes that delocalize the lone pair lower it. Aniline (\( \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 \), conjugate acid pKa 4.6) is a much weaker base than cyclohexylamine (conjugate acid pKa 10.6) because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic ring.

### Factors that tune acid and base strength

- **Electronegativity:** across a row, more electronegative atoms hold negative charge better — \( \text{HF} > \text{H}_2\text{O} > \text{NH}_3 > \text{CH}_4 \) in acidity.
- **Resonance:** stabilizes conjugate bases (carboxylate, phenoxide) and destabilizes lone pairs (aniline, amides) — the single largest effect in organic acids.
- **Inductive effects:** electron-withdrawing groups (Cl, F, \( \text{NO}_2 \)) near the acidic site stabilize the conjugate base and raise acidity. Chloroacetic acid (pKa 2.87) is stronger than acetic acid (4.76); trifluoroacetic acid (pKa 0.5) is nearly a strong acid.
- **Hybridization:** the more s-character in the orbital holding the lone pair or the C–H bond, the more electronegative the atom and the more acidic the proton. Acetylene (\( \text{sp} \), pKa 25) is far more acidic than ethylene (\( \text{sp}^2 \), pKa 44), which is more acidic than ethane (\( \text{sp}^3 \), pKa 50).
- **Solvation:** in water, small conjugate bases are stabilized by hydrogen bonding with solvent; this is why \( \text{F}^- \) is not as basic as size trends predict in water.

### Amino acids: acids and bases in one molecule

Glycine, \( \text{H}_2\text{N}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COOH} \), contains both a basic amine and an acidic carboxylic acid. In neutral water it exists as a **zwitterion**, \( {}^+\text{H}_3\text{N}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COO}^- \), with the proton transferred from the carboxyl group to the amine. The carboxyl group donates its proton (pKa ≈ 2.3) and the ammonium group holds it (pKa ≈ 9.6), so amino acids are buffered over a wide pH range — the reason proteins and peptides resist pH change in the body.

## ELI-10: Explain Like I'm 10

> Some molecules want to give away a hydrogen atom (acids), and some want to grab one (bases). Organic acids are like people with an extra umbrella they're happy to lend — but only if letting go makes them feel more stable, like spreading the "crowd" of electrons over more space. Carboxylic acids spread the crowd over two oxygens, so they lend easily; alcohols can't spread it, so they hold on tight. Amines are the borrowers: they love to grab a hydrogen because it makes them positively charged and stable.

## High-Yield Points

- Carboxylic acids: pKa ≈ 4–5 (resonance-stabilized carboxylate). Phenols: pKa ≈ 10 (ring resonance). Alcohols: pKa ≈ 16–18 (no resonance).
- Basicity is judged by the conjugate acid's pKa: higher \( \text{p}K_a(\text{BH}^+) \) = stronger base. Alkylamine conjugate acids pKa ≈ 10–11; anilinium pKa ≈ 4.6.
- Resonance stabilizes conjugate bases → more acidic parent; resonance on the base itself → less basic (aniline, amides, pyrrole).
- Inductive electron withdrawal raises acidity: \( \text{ClCH}_2\text{COOH} \) (2.87) > \( \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \) (4.76); \( \text{CF}_3\text{COOH} \) ≈ 0.5.
- Hybridization: more s-character, more acidic — \( \text{sp} \) alkyne (25) > \( \text{sp}^2 \) alkene (44) > \( \text{sp}^3 \) alkane (50).
- Amino acids are zwitterions in neutral water: \( {}^+\text{H}_3\text{N}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COO}^- \). The carboxyl pKa ≈ 2.3, ammonium pKa ≈ 9.6.
- Protonated alcohols/ethers (\( \text{p}K_a \approx -2 \) to −3) are excellent leaving groups — acid catalysis converts \( \text{ROH} \) into \( \text{ROH}_2^+ \).

## Key Terms

| Term | Plain-Language Definition | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|
| Organic acid | A carbon-containing proton donor (RCOOH, ArOH, ROH, RC≡CH, RNH–) | The tunable acidity of these families is central to reactivity and drug behavior |
| Organic base | A carbon-containing proton acceptor, typically an amine \( \text{R}_3\text{N} \) | Amines are the workhorse organic bases; their strength varies with substitution and resonance |
| Carboxylic acid | \( \text{RCOOH} \); the archetypal organic acid, pKa ≈ 4–5 | The most common acidic group in drugs, amino acids, and metabolism |
| Conjugate base | What remains after an acid loses a proton | Its stability determines the acid's strength |
| Zwitterion | A neutral molecule with both + and − charges | The form of amino acids at physiological pH; explains their solubility and buffering |
| Inductive effect | Electron withdrawal/push through sigma bonds by nearby atoms | Withdrawing groups raise acidity (Cl, F, NO₂); donating groups lower it |
| s-character | Fraction of s orbital in a hybrid (sp > sp² > sp³) | Higher s-character = more electronegative = more acidic C–H |
| Amine salt | \( \text{R}_3\text{NH}^+ \text{X}^- \), formed by protonating an amine | Converts oily amines into water-soluble solids — used in drug formulation and extraction |

## Worked Examples

### Example 1: Why is acetic acid so much stronger than ethanol?

**Problem:** Rank \( \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \) (pKa 4.76), \( \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \) (pKa 10), and \( \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \) (pKa 16) in order of acidity and explain the gaps.

**Plan and formula:** acidity follows conjugate-base stability, which follows the number of resonance forms and the electronegativity of the atom carrying the charge. Count the resonance stabilization of each conjugate base:

- **Acetate, \( \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- \):** the negative charge is shared equally between two oxygen atoms (two equivalent resonance forms). Strongest stabilization → most acidic.
- **Phenoxide, \( \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^- \):** charge delocalizes onto the oxygen and onto ortho/para ring carbons. Intermediate stabilization → intermediate acidity.
- **Ethoxide, \( \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^- \):** no resonance; the charge sits entirely on one oxygen. Weakest stabilization → least acidic.

**Answer:** \( \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} > \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} > \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \). Quantitatively, acetic acid is \( 10^{16 - 4.76} \approx 10^{11} \) times more acidic than ethanol — an enormous difference driven entirely by resonance.

### Example 2: Which is the stronger base — aniline or cyclohexylamine?

**Problem:** Compare the basicity of aniline, \( \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 \), and cyclohexylamine, \( \text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{NH}_2 \). Conjugate acid pKas: \( \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_3^+ \) = 4.6; \( \text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{NH}_3^+ \) = 10.6.

**Plan and formula:** base strength is proportional to conjugate-acid stability, i.e., the pKa of \( \text{BH}^+ \). Higher \( \text{p}K_a(\text{BH}^+) \) = stronger base. Compare the two values:

\[ \text{p}K_a(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{NH}_3^+) = 10.6 > \text{p}K_a(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_3^+) = 4.6 \]

**Explanation:** in aniline, the nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic ring (resonance with the π system), so it is less available for protonation; the conjugate acid \( \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_3^+ \) is correspondingly less stabilized. In cyclohexylamine the lone pair is localized on nitrogen, fully available, and the ammonium ion is well stabilized by solvation. **Answer:** cyclohexylamine is the stronger base by about \( 10^6 \) — aniline is roughly \( 10^6 \) times weaker than a typical alkylamine.

### Example 3: Which amine is a stronger base — ammonia or methylamine?

**Problem:** Compare \( \text{NH}_3 \) (\( \text{p}K_a(\text{NH}_4^+) = 9.24 \)) with \( \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 \) (\( \text{p}K_a(\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+) = 10.6 \)).

**Plan and formula:** again compare conjugate-acid pKas:

\[ \text{p}K_a(\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+) = 10.6 > \text{p}K_a(\text{NH}_4^+) = 9.24 \]

**Explanation:** the methyl group is an electron-donating group (inductive effect), which stabilizes the positive charge on the protonated amine \( \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+ \). More stabilized conjugate acid → stronger base. **Answer:** methylamine is the stronger base — roughly \( 10^{1.4} \approx 25 \) times stronger than ammonia. This is why alkylamines, not ammonia, are usually the bases of choice in organic synthesis.

## Common Confusions

| Do Not Confuse | With | Difference |
|---|---|---|
| Carboxylic acids and alcohols | Both have O–H bonds | Carboxylates benefit from two-oxygen resonance (pKa 4–5); alkoxides do not (pKa 16–18). ~10¹¹ difference. |
| Basicity of the amine | pKa of the amine | Amines are bases; their strength is quoted as the pKa of the *conjugate acid* (e.g., \( \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+ \), 10.6). Higher BH⁺ pKa = stronger base. |
| Aniline basicity | Alkylamine basicity | Aniline's lone pair is ring-delocalized (BH⁺ pKa 4.6); alkylamines' lone pairs are localized (BH⁺ pKa 10–11). |
| Inductive vs resonance effects | Both affect acidity | Inductive effects act through sigma bonds and fall off with distance; resonance acts through π systems and is usually much larger. |
| Alkyne C–H acidity | Alkane C–H acidity | sp-hybridized carbon is more electronegative: acetylene pKa 25 vs ethane pKa ~50. |
| "Organic acid" = carboxylic acid only | Other organic acids | Phenols, alcohols, thiols, and terminal alkynes are also organic acids, just weaker ones. |

## Quick Review

1. Rank the acidity of \( \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \), \( \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \), and \( \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \) and give the structural reason for the ranking.
2. Why does substituting chlorine for hydrogen on the methyl group of acetic acid (giving chloroacetic acid, pKa 2.87) make the acid stronger?
3. Which is the stronger base: pyridine (conjugate acid pKa 5.2) or triethylamine (conjugate acid pKa 10.7)? By roughly how much?
4. Draw (describe) the zwitterion form of glycine and state which group holds the positive charge and which holds the negative charge at neutral pH.
5. Why is \( \text{HC}\equiv\text{CH} \) (pKa 25) so much more acidic than \( \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3 \) (pKa ~50)?

<details>
<summary>Show answers</summary>

1. \( \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \) (4.76) > \( \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \) (10) > \( \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \) (16). Acetate has two-oxygen resonance; phenoxide has ring resonance; ethoxide has no resonance.
2. Chlorine is electron-withdrawing (inductive effect). It pulls electron density away from the carboxylate ion, stabilizing the negative charge, which raises acidity. Two chlorines (dichloroacetic acid) are stronger still, and three (trichloroacetic acid) approach strong-acid behavior.
3. Triethylamine is stronger. \( \Delta \text{p}K_a = 10.7 - 5.2 = 5.5 \), so triethylamine is about \( 10^{5.5} \approx 3 \times 10^5 \) times stronger. Alkyl groups donate electron density that stabilizes the conjugate acid.
4. \( {}^+\text{H}_3\text{N}-\text{CH}_2-\text{COO}^- \): the protonated amino group (\( -\text{NH}_3^+ \)) carries the positive charge and the carboxylate (\( -\text{COO}^- \)) carries the negative charge.
5. Hybridization: the sp carbon of acetylene is more electronegative than the sp³ carbon of ethane because the sp orbital has more s-character (50% vs 25%), so the C–H bond is more polar and the proton is more readily lost.

</details>
